title: WHY MOSES TOOK HIS WIFE AND SONS BACK TO MIDIAN
paragraphs: WHY MOSES TOOK HIS WIFE AND SONS BACK TO MIDIAN
The Family Moses Brought Toward Egypt Suddenly Disappears From the Story—And One Hebrew Phrase Reveals a Painful Chapter the Bible Never Fully Explains
There is a moment in the life of Moses that most people read straight past.
God had called him from the burning bush.
Egypt was waiting.
Pharaoh was waiting.
Israel was groaning.
History was about to split open beneath the footsteps of one reluctant shepherd carrying the command of God.
And Moses did not initially leave Midian alone.
Exodus says:
“So Moses took his wife and his sons and had them ride on a donkey, and went back to the land of Egypt. And Moses took God’s staff in his hand.”
—Exodus 4:20
His wife was there.
His sons were there.
They were headed toward Egypt with him.
Then something terrifying happened on the road.
And afterward...
Zipporah and the boys seem to vanish from the Exodus narrative.

By the time Moses confronts Pharaoh, stretches out the staff, watches Egypt collapse beneath the judgments of God, walks through the divided sea, and leads Israel into the wilderness, we hear virtually nothing about his wife and sons.
Then Exodus 18 quietly opens a door.
And behind that door is one Hebrew expression that has caused readers to ask a haunting question for generations.
What happened to Moses’ family?
Why were they back in Midian?
And what happened between the man God was preparing to use publicly...
and the family traveling beside him privately?
The Bible gives us part of the answer.
But not all of it.
And sometimes spiritual maturity begins when we refuse to pretend God said something He did not say.
Exodus 18:1–2 tells us that Jethro, Moses’ father-in-law, heard everything God had done for Moses and Israel. Then we read:
“Now Jethro, Moses’ father-in-law, had taken Zipporah, Moses’ wife, after he had sent her away...”
The Hebrew behind that final expression is striking.
אַחַר שִׁלּוּחֶיהָ
’achar shillucheha.
Literally, the phrase carries the sense of “after her sending away” or “after she had been sent away.”
The noun שִׁלּוּחִים and its related forms come from the Hebrew root שׁלח, shalach—“to send.”
That matters.
But we need to be careful.
Exodus does not give us a scene saying, “Then Moses sent Zipporah and his sons back to Midian because...”
There is no verse completing that sentence for us.
We know Moses originally took his wife and sons toward Egypt.
We know that later Zipporah and the children were with Jethro.
We know Exodus 18 refers to her “sending away.”
We know Jethro subsequently brought Zipporah and Moses’ sons back to Moses in the wilderness.
What Scripture does not tell us is precisely when Moses sent them away or exactly why.
That silence is important.
Because the temptation is enormous to fill biblical silence with confident imagination and then call our imagination biblical truth.
We should not.
But the sequence Scripture does reveal is extraordinary.
Immediately after Moses begins his return journey toward Egypt, one of the strangest and most frightening incidents in his entire life occurs.
“At a lodging place on the way the LORD met him and sought to put him to death.”
—Exodus 4:24
Read that again.
Moses had just been commissioned by God.
Moses had encountered the burning bush.
Moses was carrying the staff through which signs would soon be performed.
Moses was traveling under divine assignment.
And suddenly the LORD confronted him in a way so severe that the text says He “sought to put him to death.”
Calling did not make Moses exempt from obedience.
That truth should disturb every person who has ever confused being used by God with being right before God.
You can have a calling and still have an area that must be confronted.
You can know Scripture and still have something at home you have neglected.
You can speak publicly about obedience while God is putting His finger on private disobedience.
You can carry the staff...
and still need repentance.
Then Zipporah acts.
“Then Zipporah took a flint and cut off her son’s foreskin and touched Moses’ feet with it and said, ‘Surely you are a bridegroom of blood to me!’”
—Exodus 4:25
Her Hebrew words are unforgettable:
כִּי חֲתַן־דָּמִים אַתָּה לִי
ki chatan-damim attah li.
“Surely a bridegroom of blood you are to me.”
Then Scripture says that God let him alone.

The passage is difficult, and interpreters have debated some of its details for centuries, including precisely whom God confronted, whose “feet” were touched, and the exact nuance of Zipporah’s words.
But the connection with circumcision is unmistakable.
Centuries earlier, God had established circumcision as the sign of His covenant with Abraham and his descendants.
God had said:
“Every male among you shall be circumcised.”
—Genesis 17:10
And concerning an uncircumcised male:
“that person shall be cut off from his people; he has broken my covenant.”
—Genesis 17:14
Now think about the staggering irony.
Moses was being sent to confront Pharaoh concerning God’s covenant people.
Moses was about to announce judgment in the name of the covenant-keeping God.
Moses was about to lead Abraham’s descendants out of slavery.
Yet within Moses’ own household, the covenant sign had apparently not been administered to at least one of his sons.
Before Moses could stand before Pharaoh...
God confronted Moses.
Before the public battle came the private reckoning.
Before Egypt saw the staff...
Moses’ household encountered the holiness of God.
That is uncomfortable Christianity.
We love stories in which God confronts Pharaoh.
We become much quieter when God confronts Moses.
We love preaching about the sins of Egypt.
It becomes painful when the Word walks into our own house.
Our hidden compromise.
Our neglected obedience.
Our bitterness.
Our secret addiction.
Our dishonest business practice.
Our pornography.
Our pride.
Our unforgiveness.
Our double life.
The version of us everybody applauds...
and the version only God sees.
Maybe you have been asking God to defeat your Pharaoh while God has been trying to deal with something inside you.
That does not mean every hardship is punishment for secret sin. Scripture does not allow us to make that cruel assumption.
But it does mean God cares about the holiness of the person He calls.
And grace does not make obedience irrelevant.
Grace transforms the forgiven into people who increasingly desire to obey the One who saved them.
What happened immediately afterward between Moses and Zipporah?
Scripture does not say.
We must honor that silence.

Some interpreters have connected Zipporah’s later return to Midian with this frightening circumcision episode. It is certainly possible that Moses decided his family should return to the relative safety of Jethro’s household before he entered the dangerous confrontation awaiting him in Egypt. Others have suggested different circumstances.
But possibility is not revelation.
We cannot preach the missing scene as though we witnessed it.
We cannot know whether there was an argument beside that lodging place.
We cannot know whether Zipporah was angry, terrified, bewildered, or simply exhausted beyond words.
We cannot know whether Moses immediately sent them back or whether the separation happened later.
We cannot know whether danger in Egypt was the decisive reason.
The Bible does not tell us.
And perhaps that very silence makes what happens in Exodus 18 even more beautiful.
Because after Pharaoh...
after the plagues...
after Passover...
after blood appeared on Israelite doorposts...
after the sea opened...
after Egypt’s armies disappeared beneath the waters...
after Moses became the human face of one of the greatest deliverances recorded in Scripture...
someone came walking toward him through the wilderness.
Jethro.
And he was not alone.
“Jethro, Moses’ father-in-law, came with his sons and his wife to Moses in the wilderness where he was encamped at the mountain of God.”
—Exodus 18:5
His wife came back.
His children came back.
The family that disappeared from the narrative reappeared.
And even the names of Moses’ sons preach.
One was Gershom.
Exodus explains the name because Moses said:
“I have been a sojourner in a foreign land.”
The other was Eliezer.
“For he said, ‘The God of my father was my help, and delivered me from the sword of Pharaoh.’”
—Exodus 18:4
Gershom carried the memory of exile.
Eliezer carried the testimony of deliverance.
Alienation and rescue.
Wandering and help.
Pain and mercy.
Those themes run through Moses’ life.
And they run through ours.
Maybe that is why this strange family episode feels painfully human.
The heroes of Scripture were not plastic saints floating three feet above ordinary life.
They had marriages.
Children.
Fear.
Consequences.
Misunderstandings.
Failures.
Complicated homes.
Moments Scripture leaves unresolved.
Moses could stand before Pharaoh and still have a complicated family story.
He could lead millions and still carry memories of Midian.
He could be used powerfully by God without having a spotless biography.
That does not excuse sin.
It magnifies grace.
And Moses himself was never the final Hero anyway.
Another Deliverer was coming.
A greater One.
Jesus Christ.
Moses led enslaved people out of Egypt.
Jesus delivers sinners from slavery to sin.
Moses mediated the old covenant.
Jesus is the Mediator of the new covenant.
Moses lifted his staff as waters opened.
Jesus stretched out His hands on a cross as the way to reconciliation with God was opened through His blood.
Moses was nearly destroyed in a passage centered upon covenant obligation and blood.
At Calvary, the sinless Son of God willingly gave His own blood for covenant breakers.
That is where this story ultimately has to take us.
Not to Moses.
To Christ.
Because our deepest problem is not that we have a messy family history.
It is not merely that we have made poor decisions.
It is not merely that we need to become more disciplined religious people.
Our deepest problem is sin.
We have broken God's commands.
We have loved other things more than Him.
We have hidden what we should confess.
We have justified what we should repent of.
And no amount of Christian appearance can wash away guilt before a holy God.
But Jesus can.
The scandal of the Gospel is that the Holy One receives guilty people not because their record suddenly becomes respectable, but because Christ bore the judgment sinners deserved.
“At the right time Christ died for the ungodly.”
—Romans 5:6
Not the impressive.
Not the polished.
Not the people who finally managed to clean themselves up.
The ungodly.
Then comes one of the most astonishing declarations in the New Testament:
“God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
—Romans 5:8
While we were still sinners.
There is the scandal.
And there is the grace.
Jesus does not tell you to rewrite your past before coming to Him.
He calls you to repent and believe.
He forgives.
He cleanses.
He changes hearts.
He restores what sin has shattered according to His wisdom.
He teaches His people obedience not as the purchase price of salvation, but as the fruit of a life rescued by grace.
Maybe your own story has a chapter you wish the Bible of your life could simply skip.
A marriage strained almost beyond recognition.
A child who barely speaks to you.
A secret nobody at church knows.
Years you cannot recover.
A decision you would give anything to reverse.
A season when you knew what God wanted...
and did something else.
You cannot travel backward.
Moses could not either.
But you can turn toward Christ now.
Repentance does not mean pretending yesterday never happened.
It means agreeing with God about your sin, turning from it, and running toward the mercy offered in Jesus Christ.
Some consequences may remain.
Some relationships may require years of patient rebuilding.
Some people may not reconcile.
Some scars will still be visible.
The Gospel never promises that every earthly consequence disappears.
It promises something infinitely deeper:
“There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.”
—Romans 8:1
No condemnation.
Not because the scandal was imaginary.
Because the judgment was answered at the cross.
That is grace.
And perhaps someone reading this has spent years thinking your worst chapter disqualified you from ever being useful to God again.
Look at Moses.
Do not use him as permission to remain in sin.
Use his story as evidence that failure does not have to have the final word when God intervenes.
Then look beyond Moses.
Look at Peter after denial.
Look at Paul after persecution.
Look at the thief beside Christ.
Then look directly at Jesus.
Wounded.
Crucified.
Risen.
Alive.
The Gospel is not God pretending sinners never sinned.
It is God dealing with sin at unimaginable cost and giving undeserving sinners a new standing in Christ.
From scandal...
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Be sincere before God first. Confess your sin to Him. Turn toward Christ.
And if these words describe where your heart genuinely is, comment, “Jesus, forgive me.”
If you are exhausted but still fighting for your faith, comment, “I’m still fighting.”
Sometimes one honest sentence is the beginning of a conversation someone has been afraid to have for years.
And do not keep this article trapped on your screen.
Send it privately to the person who would never admit publicly that their family is hurting.
Save it too.
There may come a night when the accusation in your own mind becomes louder than your memory of grace, and you will need these Scriptures again.
It does not.
Not because giving money purchases spiritual blessing.
It cannot.
Scripture teaches no such thing.
We glorify God through lives surrendered to Christ, and Christian generosity should be voluntary, sincere, and never coerced. As Paul wrote, “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7).
Let it be because you believe Scripture should keep traveling.
Because somebody is scrolling tonight with tears nobody knows about.
Somebody thinks their scandal is stronger than Christ's grace.
Somebody thinks the chapter they ruined must be the final chapter.
Help us reach them.
Not as a transaction with God.
As mission.
Leave an honest comment.
Save these Scriptures.
Invite someone else to follow.
Because the Gospel was never meant to terminate with the person who received it.
And before you leave, remember the strange road Moses traveled.
A burning bush behind him.
Egypt before him.
A family beside him.
A terrifying confrontation with holiness.
A wife and children later found back in Midian.
A reunion in the wilderness.
A calling that survived human weakness.
And eventually, generations later, a Savior whom Moses could only anticipate.
Maybe you have your own Midian.
Your own missing chapter.
Your own night you cannot explain.
Your own mistake you wish you could erase.
Your own family story that does not fit neatly inside a testimony.
Bring the truth into the light.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Ask forgiveness where forgiveness must be asked.
Make restitution where righteousness requires it.
Stop calling compromise “complicated.”
Stop confusing shame with repentance.
And stop believing the lie that Jesus came only for people whose stories remained clean.
He came for sinners.
He died for sinners.
He rose for sinners.
And everyone who truly comes to Him in repentant faith finds something far greater than a rewritten reputation.
They find reconciliation with God.
Your darkest chapter does not become beautiful because it was never scandalous; it becomes a testimony when the grace of Jesus is allowed to have the final word.
